title: Pour strong sulfuric acid on sugar and a black column of carbon climbs out

cover.alt: A glass beaker filled with a black, lumpy mixture that is starting to bubble up towards the rim.

body: Table sugar, sucrose, is C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁: twelve carbon atoms plus exactly the hydrogen and oxygen needed for eleven molecules of water. Concentrated **sulfuric acid** pulls water out of other compounds so strongly that it strips those atoms away, leaving black carbon behind. The reaction releases a lot of heat, which turns the water into steam, and the steam and other gases, such as carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide, puff the carbon up into a rigid, porous column that rises out of the glass.

slides.alt: A beaker full of a black, glistening mixture foams at the top, then a lumpy black mass swells up over the rim and keeps growing upwards as the camera tilts up to follow it.
slides.caption: Sugar soaked in concentrated sulfuric acid has turned black. Now it foams and pushes a column of porous carbon up out of the beaker.

slides.heading: Of the 45 atoms in a sugar molecule, 33 can leave as water
slides.note: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁: 22 hydrogens and 11 oxygens make 11 H₂O, leaving 12 carbons

slides.heading: From white sugar to black foam

steps.label: Concentrated acid soaks into the sugar
The acid pulls water out of the sugar
Heat turns that water into steam
Gases puff the carbon into a tall column

slides.heading: Acid into water, never the reverse
slides.text: Sulfuric acid grabs water so eagerly that mixing the two releases a lot of heat. That is why chemists add the acid to water and avoid pouring water into the acid: the heat can boil the solution and spray out droplets of hot acid.

slides.question: What does a splash of concentrated sulfuric acid do to paper?
slides.explanation: It pulls water out of the paper’s cellulose too, leaving carbon that looks much like soot from a fire.
